Fall 2026 @ Carnegie Mellon University

HomeScheduleAssignmentsProjectSyllabus & PoliciesStaffSponsorship

Course Overview

This course studies LLM-based AI agents: systems that use large language models to perceive, reason, plan, and act over many steps. Agents interact with their environments — calling tools, navigating interfaces, writing code, working alongside people — to complete real tasks.

The course covers both the foundations of building agents and active research questions around long-horizon reasoning, training, safety, and interaction. We emphasize hands-on implementation with modern frameworks and the training methods that make agents more capable and reliable.

  • Graham Neubig - Instructor

Fall 2026 @ Carnegie Mellon University

HomeScheduleAssignmentsProjectSyllabus & PoliciesStaffSponsorship

Research Project

Work in a team of 2–4 students to make a novel contribution to LLM-based agents. Develop a focused idea, study relevant prior work, implement and evaluate your approach, and communicate what you learn. The project has three components: Project Hours, Poster Presentation, and Report.

The course policies apply to collaboration, submission, academic integrity, and AI tool use. Every teammate should make a substantive contribution and understand the project as a whole.

Project components and weights in the final course grade
ComponentCourse gradeFormat
Project Hours5%Team of 2–4
Poster Presentation15%Team of 2–4
Report30%Team of 2–4
Project scopeProject HoursPoster PresentationReportFAQ

Project scope and expectations

Aim for work at or close to the level of a workshop submission: a focused novel contribution, meaningful experiments, and thoughtful analysis. Keep the scope manageable, for example by focusing on a few models, a limited set of tasks, and a few well-chosen experiments or analyses. We do not expect experimental evidence at the scale or scope of a full conference submission in this project, although if your results are promising your work could lay a foundation for one.

Expect to spend approximately 9 hours per week per person on the project now that the assignments are complete. When grading, we will account for your team size and the roughly one-month project timeline.

Project Hours

Thu, Nov 5, 2026, during class time (3:30–4:50 PM). Meet with your assigned TA as a team to discuss your research plan and get early feedback. Each team has a 10-minute slot. Aim to present for 6–7 minutes, leaving the remaining time for questions and discussion.

See the Project Hours post on Piazza for your group’s room and time assignment. Room assignments are organized by TA.

Prepare a concise presentation covering:

  • Research topic: What question are you investigating, and why does it matter?
  • Related work: What are the most relevant prior results, and what gap or opportunity do you see?
  • Experimental plan: What tasks, data, baselines, and evaluation metrics will you use? Cite the work behind your comparisons and check that the experiments fit your compute and API budget.
  • Proposed approach: What will you try, and what specific experiment would test your idea?

We recommend preparing slides and presenting from a teammate’s laptop.

Grading

Project Hours are primarily an opportunity for feedback. Grading is based on completion: address all four topics above to receive full credit, with each topic worth one quarter of the Project Hours grade. Every team member must attend and participate. A team member who misses Project Hours receives zero for this component.

Poster Presentation

Tue, Dec 1 and Thu, Dec 3, 2026, during class time (3:30–4:50 PM). Present your project in person during your team’s assigned poster session. Use the session to practice explaining the work, learn about classmates’ projects, and gather feedback to improve your report.

Your poster should make three things easy to understand:

  • The problem and why it matters.
  • Your approach and experimental setup.
  • Your results and the main lessons from them.

Choose a readable layout with clear figures and concise text. A three-column layout organized around the problem, method, and results is one option; there is no required poster template.

Grading

The poster is graded pass/fail based on completing a poster and attending your assigned session to present it. Every team member must attend and participate to receive credit.

Report

Due Friday, December 4, 2026, at 11:59 PM. You may use up to three late days to submit without penalty through Monday, December 7, 2026, at 11:59 PM. Submissions after that time will not be accepted.

Carry out the project and refine your approach as you learn from experiments and feedback. Write a research report that explains the question, the work you completed, and the evidence supporting your conclusions.

Report contents

Abstract
Summarize the research question, why it matters, your approach, the main findings, and the contribution.
Introduction
Explain the problem in AI agents and the gap that motivates your work. Introduce your approach and give a brief overview of the results and insights.
Related Work
Situate the project in the relevant research landscape. Discuss the closest studies in enough detail to explain how your work builds on them and which limitations or open questions it addresses.
Data
Describe your tasks, environments, and datasets, including their sources, sizes, domains, and splits. Explain why they suit your research question and document any collection, annotation, filtering, or preprocessing.
Method
Describe your approach and comparison baselines, justify the design choices, and explain your experimental setup and evaluation metrics. Include the model, agent harness, tools, training or inference procedure, compute budget, and hyperparameters needed to understand and reproduce the work. Additional implementation details may go in the appendix.
Results
Present the evidence for your claims using tables, plots, and concrete examples. Compare against appropriate baselines, report uncertainty or significance where appropriate, and analyze failures as well as successes. Include qualitative findings when relevant.
Discussion
Interpret the findings in relation to your research question. Explain the strengths and weaknesses of the approach, unexpected behavior, and what the results imply for building or studying agents.
Conclusion & Future Work
State the main takeaway and its significance beyond your particular setup. Identify useful follow-up experiments or research directions.
Limitations
Explain the boundaries of the evidence: constraints in the data, tasks, models, resources, or evaluation, and settings to which the findings may not generalize.
Ethical Considerations
Discuss relevant risks from the agent’s capabilities, tool access, data, or deployment. Address privacy, bias, potential misuse, and safeguards where applicable.
Team Member Contributions
Describe each team member’s contributions to the project, including implementation, experiments, analysis, and writing.

Submission

Submit a PDF report through Canvas, written in LaTeX using ACL format. Aim for 6–9 pages of main text, with a maximum of 9 pages. References and an optional appendix do not count toward this limit. Length itself earns no credit; do not pad a complete, concise report to reach nine pages. Follow the course submission policies and ensure any submitted repository links are accessible to course staff. Describe each team member’s contribution to the project.

Grading

The report is evaluated on the clarity and completeness of the sections above, the motivation and scope of the research question, the quality of the implementation and experiments, and the depth of the analysis. Explain what you completed and support your claims with evidence.

FAQ

Can I use AI tools for the project?

Yes. You may use AI tools for your project, consistent with the course policy on AI tools. You are responsible for the accuracy of your work and for understanding all submitted code, methods, results, and writing. We will test your understanding of your project through the poster presentation, and we may interview you about your report after you have submitted it.

How much space in the report should we allocate to each subsection?

There is no fixed allocation across sections. Spend space on the details needed to understand your contribution and evidence, while staying within the overall page limit. Papers on similar topics can help you judge the balance. Use an appendix for supporting material rather than essential claims or results.

How can I use late days for the project?

You may use up to three late days for the Report, which is due Friday, December 4, 2026, at 11:59 PM. Reports submitted by Monday, December 7, 2026, at 11:59 PM incur no penalty; submissions after that time will not be accepted. You cannot use late days for Project Hours or the Poster Presentation.

Team issues / Unfair Distribution of Work / Team Changes

Communicate regularly and agree on responsibilities with your teammates. Try to resolve disagreements within the team first. If a problem continues or a team change is needed, contact the instructors promptly so they can help and assess contributions fairly.

Project Hours/Poster Session Conflicts

Attendance and participation in person are required for both Project Hours and your assigned poster session. Missing either event results in zero for that component. If you have a serious conflict, contact course staff in advance through a private post on Piazza and include your team name. Exceptional circumstances will be considered individually in accordance with course policies.

Poster Printing

Arrange printing early enough to bring a printed poster to your session. Check the printing service’s file requirements and turnaround time before submitting your PDF. Contact the TAs in advance if you need help arranging printing.

Negative Results

A carefully executed project can earn a good grade even when the proposed approach does not improve the results. Explain the hypothesis and why it was plausible, document the experiments, and investigate why the outcome differed from your expectations. Strong analysis and clear evidence of a serious research effort are especially valuable here.

Adapted from the Spring 2026 Advanced NLP project guidance.

Syllabus

Prerequisites

  • Prior experience training neural language models.
  • Recommended background includes 11-667, 11-711, 10-202, or equivalent experience.

Class Format

The first half of the course emphasizes individual implementation assignments on core agent capabilities and domains. The second half centers on a team-based mini research project on advanced agent topics.

Target Audience

Graduate students with prior experience training neural language models. Relevant background includes coursework such as 11-667, 11-711, or 10-202, or equivalent experience.

Course Themes

  • Agent Capabilities: Instruction following, tool use, planning, and memory systems.
  • Application Domains: General tool use, coding agents, GUI agents, and social agents.
  • Training Methods: Supervised fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning algorithms and systems.
  • Frameworks: OpenHands, LangGraph, and other agent development frameworks.
  • Safety: Sandboxing, credentialing, and adversarial attacks on agents.
  • Advanced Topics: Human-agent interaction, multi-agent systems, and search-based reasoning.

What You'll Learn

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  • Implement an agent from scratch on top of an open-source LLM.
  • Design evaluations for multi-step tasks.
  • Train agents to improve their capabilities.
  • Reason about safety and reliability tradeoffs.
  • Pursue an open research question in agents.

Grading

ComponentWeightFormat
Assignment 1: Harness10%Individual
Assignment 2: Eval15%Individual
Assignment 3: Training15%Individual
Lecture highlights10%Individual
Project Hours5%Team of 2–4
Poster Presentation15%Team of 2–4
Report30%Team of 2–4

Related Courses

Courses with overlapping content that students may also consider:

  • 11-711: Advanced NLP — Roughly two weeks on RL and agents, with stronger emphasis on RL methods.
  • 11-766: Large Language Model Applications — Roughly two weeks on agent-adjacent applications such as tool calling, security, multi-agent systems, and code assistants.
  • 11-891: Neural Code Generation — Roughly two weeks on code generation agents.
  • 11-777: Multimodal Machine Learning — Roughly one week on GUI agents.

Course Policies

The assignments and research project are designed to build the implementation, evaluation, and research skills needed to create capable and reliable LLM-based agents. By the end of the course, students should be able to build an agent on top of an open-source language model, evaluate it on multi-step tasks, train it, and investigate an open research question.

Read each assignment and project description carefully. You are responsible for following all instructions, including requirements about permitted resources, collaboration, formats, and deadlines. Individual and team work

Assignments 1–3 must be completed individually. You may discuss course concepts and general approaches with classmates, but the code, analysis, and writing you submit must be your own unless an assignment explicitly permits additional collaboration. Do not share solutions or view another student's solution.

The research project must be completed in a team of 2–4 students. Project teammates may share code, writing, results, and ideas with one another. Each teammate is expected to understand the entire submission and to make a substantive contribution. Course staff may use project materials, version history, and conversations with the team to understand individual contributions.

If you have difficulty finding a project team, contact the course staff by the team-formation deadline. We will help match ungrouped students.

Submission

Unless an assignment description says otherwise, submit work through Canvas by the posted deadline. Each description will specify the required materials, which may include source code, system outputs or evaluation results, a PDF report, and a link to a code repository.

You are responsible for confirming that:

  • all required files are present, correctly named, and readable;
  • the submitted archive opens successfully;
  • repository links are accessible to the course staff by the deadline, including when the repository is private;
  • the submitted code runs in the required environment; and
  • the submission does not contain credentials, private data, model API keys, or other secrets.

The version received through the designated submission system is the version that will be graded. Submit early enough to correct upload, permission, or packaging problems before the deadline.

Late work and slack days

Each of Assignments 1–3 includes two slack days. A slack day is a 24-hour extension and may be used without advance permission. Slack days are attached to each assignment: they cannot be transferred between assignments, shared with another student, or applied to another course component. Any part of a 24-hour period counts as one slack day.

After both slack days for an assignment have been used, 5% of that assignment's total possible score will be deducted for each additional day or part of a day that it is late.

The project Report is due Friday, December 4, 2026, at 11:59 PM and allows up to three late days without penalty, through Monday, December 7, 2026, at 11:59 PM. Report submissions after that time will not be accepted. No late days may be used for Project Hours or the Poster Presentation.

Documented health conditions, disability accommodations, religious observances, and other circumstances covered by university policy will be handled in accordance with CMU policy. Job interviews, recruiting events, routine personal travel, and other ordinary personal conflicts are not excused absences. Plan these activities around class whenever possible. For other serious or exceptional circumstances, contact the instructors as soon as reasonably possible.

Lecture highlights

After each eligible lecture, submit a lecture highlight through the corresponding Canvas quiz within 24 hours after the lecture ends. A lecture highlight should contain one thoughtful takeaway or question that demonstrates engagement with the lecture. It should be specific enough to show what idea, argument, method, result, or unresolved issue prompted your response. A generic summary or a statement that could have been written without attending or reviewing the lecture will not receive credit.

There will be 22 opportunities to submit lecture highlights, and this portion of the grade will be calculated from 20 submissions. The two additional opportunities provide built-in flexibility for occasional absences for any reason. If an excused absence affects additional submissions, contact the course staff promptly so that an appropriate accommodation can be arranged.

Lecture highlights are graded for timely, thoughtful engagement, not for agreeing with the instructors or asking a question with a known answer. Because they are intended to capture your own engagement with the class, the response you submit must be written by you rather than generated by another person or an AI tool.

Use of AI tools

You may generally use AI tools to assist with assignments and project report work unless a particular assignment or project description restricts or prohibits their use. We prohibit AI tools for lecture highlights. Assignment-specific rules always take precedence over this general permission.

Regardless of how AI tools are used, you are responsible for:

  • the accuracy and validity of every claim, result, citation, and piece of code you submit;
  • complying with all requirements and restrictions in the assignment or project description;
  • understanding all submitted code, methods, analyses, and writing; and
  • ensuring that your submission represents permitted work and does not incorporate another student's solution or otherwise violate academic-integrity rules.

AI output is not an authoritative source. Check generated code and factual claims, verify citations against the original sources, and test all submitted work. You may not use an AI tool to bypass a requirement that you implement, analyze, or write something yourself.

We will assess your understanding through quizzes about the assignments and project reports. You may be asked to explain design decisions, code behavior, experimental results, limitations, or written claims in your submission. You are responsible for being able to explain and defend the work even when an AI tool helped produce or revise part of it.

Academic integrity, external resources, and code reuse

All course work is governed by the Carnegie Mellon University academic-integrity policy. Violations may result in penalties including no credit for the work, failure of the course, and university disciplinary action.

Unless an assignment explicitly says otherwise:

  • Code, pseudocode, templates, and starter materials supplied by the instructors or TAs may be used for that assignment.
  • When an assignment asks you to implement a method, you may not substitute an existing implementation written by someone else for your own work.
  • You may not use code or solutions written by another current or former student. Project teammates may share work only within their own team for the team project.
  • Any permitted external code, data, text, figures, or ideas must be used consistently with its license and cited appropriately. A citation does not make otherwise prohibited reuse permissible.
  • Do not post assignment solutions publicly unless the instructors give permission.

If your course project may overlap with work you are doing elsewhere—for example, another course or a separate research project with individuals not in this course—consult the instructors early. Generally, they should be separate projects.

Consulting the course staff

For assignments and projects, you are free to consult with the TAs and instructors during office hours, project hours, and through Piazza. If you don't have much experience with NLP, it will be helpful to consult with the instructors and TAs to learn about how to do the assignments and course project.

Because this is a project-based course, we assume that many of the students taking the course will be interested in turning their assignments or project into research papers. In this case, if you have received useful advice from the instructor or TAs that made the project significantly better, consider inviting them to be co-authors on the paper. Of course, you do not need to do so just because the paper is a result of the class, only if you feel that their advice or help made a contribution. Do not add individuals as authors to a paper without consulting with those individuals first!
